CrossOver and Wine are already great software to run the game itself, but EAC also checks the hardware and OS it runs on, which is why Anti-Cheat protected games don't run on Mac.

A friend and I wrote a paper on a solution with practical testing: run a Linux-based system (in this case Valve's SteamOS) inside a Mac VM / app, to use Steam's Proton (which is a fork of Wine made for Linux that can run Anti-Cheat protected games) to let EAC run on Linux.

With this, we already got a few games that are Easy Anti-Cheat protected running on macOS / Apple Silicon, including online matchmaking and online play! The Good Part: Nothing is hidden. EAC was not modified and can see the virtual machine and it accepted that setup anyway.

Some caveats: - It only works for games whose developers have enabled EAC's Proton / Linux support - The first load of game assets is really slow because of Metal shader compilation (40s-50s cold, works afterwards when content is cached) - Epic Games / EAC don't officially support emulation / VMs

For the curious:

I really recommend checking out the linked paper below, but as a quick sum up: EAC's Linux client is x86-64 only, and its launcher injects it into the game using ptrace, a Linux debugging feature. So translating the CPU instructions isn't enough: the emulator (FEX-Emu) also has to reproduce Linux process tracing and signal behavior faithfully. At first it didn't, and EAC failed to start. It looked like EAC had detected the emulator, but the emulator was just getting Linux details wrong.

On the GPU side, Direct3D goes to Vulkan inside the VM, then to Metal on the Mac. The main bottleneck is shader compilation, which causes the long first load and occasional freezes. A persistent cache on the Mac helps on repeat loads.

The paper also covers CPU overhead, input latency and what didn't work.

The device with Rayhunter installed will notify you when these signatures are being detected and you get a pcap file that you can dissect using Wireshark.

There are other tools that you can install on Android devices but Rayhunter certainly is a good start if you want to detect the use of IMSI catchers.

But, let's go down the rabbit hole, eh? There are several legal theories under which an AI agent's operator can be charged:

- Direct perpetration, with the AI as the instrument. 18 USC section 2 (principals), and possibly wire fraud (18 USC Setion 1343). Under this, the law treats the defendent with using the AI as a tool (which the big AI firms argue anyway) which punishes the operator

- Criminal recklessness or even negligence - 18 USC Secion 1112 (Involuntary Manslaughter) - if someone died, the agent operator could be pursued this way

typedef struct {
      double value;
      int    error;
  } maybe_double;
Is most efficient on x86-64 SYSV, because the ABI supports the `error` being returned in a GP register, and the `value` in a vector register. The struct is returned in `rax:xmm0` - the double is where it is meant to be.

When you use a union containing an int and a double, the double has to be moved to a GP register, and back to the vector register when read as a double (via movq), so there's a small hidden cost compared to the former approach. Your `Result_double` is returned in `rax:rdx`.

There's a trick you can use to avoid this - keep the `double` in the vector register and move the `int` to the vector register instead - so you only pay the cost to move between GP and vector registers when there's an error but not otherwise. To do this, make the union use `__m64` instead of `int` - the whole union is then in a vector register, and the `Result_double` struct is returned in `rax:xmm0`, as with `maybe_double` struct.

   typedef struct {
        _Bool ok;
        union {
            double value;
            __m64 error;
        };
    } Result_double;
Of course, this is x86-64 SYSV only. On AARCH64, the double will always be moved to a GP register in either example. Other conventions may also differ - MSVC in particular is poor because it converts to pass-by-pointer to a stack allocated structure for any struct greater than 64-bits.
